items.stem: The sentiment expressed in the cartoon above is continuous with criticisms of all of the following federal policies from the 1900s EXCEPT
items.stimulus: King Andrew the First , Unknown Artist, c. 1833
options: (A) Franklin Roosevelt’s proposals for Supreme Court reform
(B) Richard Nixon’s use of presidential power to cover up the Watergate break-in
(C) Ronald Reagan’s funding of anti-communist forces in Nicaragua
(D) Bill Clinton’s reform of welfare laws
items.explanation: The cartoon suggests that Jackson is acting tyrannically and without regard to the Constitution. Select an answer that doesn’t fit with this criticism. For (A), Roosevelt’s court-packing plan was derided as a power grab, which lines up well with the message in the cartoon. For (B), critics pounced on Nixon’s Watergate scandal as an abuse of office, forcing him to resign. For (C), many members of Congress argued Reagan had broken the law with the Iran-Contra scandal. Choice (D) is the best option: while many criticized Clinton’s welfare reform laws, the criticism was not because Clinton lacked the constitutional authority to do so.

option_explanations.A: Roosevelt's 1937 court-packing plan was attacked as a tyrannical power grab — the same 'acting above the Constitution' criticism the cartoon levels at Jackson, so it fits, not the exception.
option_explanations.B: Nixon's use of presidential power to cover up Watergate was condemned as an abuse of office — the same tyranny criticism, so it fits, not the exception.
option_explanations.C: Reagan's funding of the Nicaraguan Contras (the Iran-Contra affair) was charged in Congress as lawbreaking by the executive — the same criticism, so it fits, not the exception.
option_explanations.D: Clinton's welfare reform (1996) was legislation passed through Congress, not a presidential power grab. It does not fit the cartoon's charge of tyrannical executive overreach — this is the exception.

items.stem: All of the following resulted from the policy referenced in the cartoon above EXCEPT
items.stimulus: King Andrew the First , Unknown Artist, c. 1833
options: (A) the depositing of federal funds in state banks
(B) land over-speculation and a massive financial panic
(C) a permanent end to federalized central banking
(D) the invigoration of a political party opposed to Jackson’s financial policies
items.explanation: This question is asking us about effects of Jackson’s Bank War, without explicitly saying it’s about the bank war. Choices (A), (B), and (D) all describe consequences of this event: Jackson redeposited funds in “pet” banks, banks began lending out far too much money, the Panic of 1837 ensued, and the Whigs successfully used the crisis to win the presidency in 1840. However, even though Jackson did kill the national bank for now, it would return in the 1900s with the Federal Reserve, making (C) the best choice.

option_explanations.A: Jackson did remove federal deposits from the Bank and place them in state 'pet' banks — a real result, not the exception.
option_explanations.B: The Bank War's financial chaos fed land speculation and helped bring on the Panic of 1837 — a real result, not the exception.
option_explanations.C: The Bank's death was not permanent. Federal central banking returned in the 1900s with the Federal Reserve System (1913) — so this is the exception.
option_explanations.D: The Whigs did capitalize on the panic and Bank War fallout, winning the presidency in 1840 — a real result, not the exception.

items.stem: The nature of both Adams’ and Polk’s excerpts above best reflect which of the following common views of the 19th century?
items.stimulus: Source 1: “The whole continent of North America appears to be destined by Divine Providence to be peopled by one nation, speaking one language, professing one general system of religious and political principles, and accustomed to one general tenor of social usages and customs. For the common happiness of them all, for their peace and prosperity, I believe it is indispensable that they should be associated in one federal Union.” Source: John Quincy Adams, letter to his father, 1811 Source 2: “In assuming responsibilities so vast I fervently invoke the aid of that Almighty Ruler of the Universe in whose hands are the destinies of nations and of men to guard this Heaven-favored land against the mischiefs which without His guidance might arise from an unwise public policy. With a firm reliance upon the wisdom of Omnipotence to sustain and direct me in the path of duty which I am appointed to pursue, I stand in the presence of this assembled multitude of my countrymen to take upon myself the solemn obligation ‘to the best of my ability to preserve, protect, and defend the Constitution of the United States.” Source: James Polk, Inauguration Speech, 1845
options: (A) Laissez-faire economics
(B) Social Darwinism
(C) Manifest Destiny
(D) Nativism
items.explanation: The vision that the “whole continent of North America…be peopled by one nation, speaking one language” aligns closely with the commonly held 19th-century view of Manifest Destiny. Laissez-faire economics, (A), was a policy of keeping economic regulation and policy out of politics. This approach to the American economy was far more common in the late 19th century during the Gilded Age. Social Darwinism, (B), was a view that only the “fittest” and strongest should see their power and wealth increase at the expense of the weak. Nativism, (D), which also extolled the vision of the United States, was more concerned with the superiority of existing Americans over the rights and influence of immigrants.

option_explanations.A: Laissez-faire economics is about keeping government out of the economy, not about a divinely destined continental nation.
option_explanations.B: Social Darwinism — the 'survival of the fittest' applied to society — belongs to the late 19th century and is about competition, not divine national mission.
option_explanations.C: Both Adams (1811) and Polk claim Divine Providence destines one American nation, one language, and one Union to overspread North America — the classic 19th-century view of Manifest Destiny.
option_explanations.D: Nativism is hostility to immigrants, not the ideology of continental expansion.

items.stem: Supporters of the point of view expressed in the second excerpt supported all of the following EXCEPT
items.stimulus: Source 1: “The whole continent of North America appears to be destined by Divine Providence to be peopled by one nation, speaking one language, professing one general system of religious and political principles, and accustomed to one general tenor of social usages and customs. For the common happiness of them all, for their peace and prosperity, I believe it is indispensable that they should be associated in one federal Union.” Source: John Quincy Adams, letter to his father, 1811 Source 2: “In assuming responsibilities so vast I fervently invoke the aid of that Almighty Ruler of the Universe in whose hands are the destinies of nations and of men to guard this Heaven-favored land against the mischiefs which without His guidance might arise from an unwise public policy. With a firm reliance upon the wisdom of Omnipotence to sustain and direct me in the path of duty which I am appointed to pursue, I stand in the presence of this assembled multitude of my countrymen to take upon myself the solemn obligation ‘to the best of my ability to preserve, protect, and defend the Constitution of the United States.” Source: James Polk, Inauguration Speech, 1845
options: (A) the annexation of Texas into the United States
(B) the addition of California and Oregon as new states
(C) war with Mexico
(D) limits on the spread of slavery into Western territories
items.explanation: Hopefully you remember that Polk is an expansionist and proslavery Democrat, meaning that (A), (B), and (C) were all events that occurred while he was president. However, the one thing that Polk’s supporters were split on was the spread of slavery. Polk himself preferred to see the institution spread, meaning (D) is the one answer that is out of place, so you should pick that one.

option_explanations.A: Polk's supporters backed the annexation of Texas (1845) — not the exception.
option_explanations.B: Polk's supporters backed acquiring California and settling Oregon — not the exception.
option_explanations.C: Polk's supporters backed the war with Mexico (1846-48) that won the Southwest — not the exception.
option_explanations.D: Polk was an expansionist and proslavery Democrat who wanted slavery to spread into new territory. Limits on slavery's expansion were what his supporters opposed — this is the exception.

items.stem: The point of view expressed by both authors would have likely been challenged by all of the following groups EXCEPT
items.stimulus: Source 1: “The whole continent of North America appears to be destined by Divine Providence to be peopled by one nation, speaking one language, professing one general system of religious and political principles, and accustomed to one general tenor of social usages and customs. For the common happiness of them all, for their peace and prosperity, I believe it is indispensable that they should be associated in one federal Union.” Source: John Quincy Adams, letter to his father, 1811 Source 2: “In assuming responsibilities so vast I fervently invoke the aid of that Almighty Ruler of the Universe in whose hands are the destinies of nations and of men to guard this Heaven-favored land against the mischiefs which without His guidance might arise from an unwise public policy. With a firm reliance upon the wisdom of Omnipotence to sustain and direct me in the path of duty which I am appointed to pursue, I stand in the presence of this assembled multitude of my countrymen to take upon myself the solemn obligation ‘to the best of my ability to preserve, protect, and defend the Constitution of the United States.” Source: James Polk, Inauguration Speech, 1845
options: (A) conservatives in the 1980s
(B) anti-imperialists in the early 1900s
(C) opponents of the Vietnam War in the 1960s
(D) Pennsylvania Quakers in the 1700s
items.explanation: Both Quincy Adams and Polk are supposing that America is uniquely favored by God and has a right to expand its influence beyond its boundaries. Anti-imperialists in the 1900s heavily criticized this idea, as did opponents of the Vietnam War, so eliminate (B) and (C). The Quakers were known for their liberal theology and relative friendliness to other faith traditions, so (D) is out too. Conservatives in the 1980s, however, argued that America had a right to intervene abroad to protect its interests in the Cold War, which fits nicely with the sentiments expressed here, so (A) is the best choice.

option_explanations.A: Conservatives in the 1980s argued America had a right and duty to intervene abroad against communism — embracing the Adams/Polk view of a divinely favored, expansive America, not challenging it. This is the exception.
option_explanations.B: Anti-imperialists of the early 1900s directly attacked the idea that America had a right to dominate others — a genuine challenge, not the exception.
option_explanations.C: Opponents of the Vietnam War challenged the interventionist creed — a genuine challenge, not the exception.
option_explanations.D: Pennsylvania Quakers, with their pacifism and religious tolerance, would reject a divinely ordained American empire — a genuine challenge, not the exception.

items.stem: Supporters of the ideology expressed in both passages above disagreed most over which of the following from 1800 to 1860?
items.stimulus: Source 1: “The whole continent of North America appears to be destined by Divine Providence to be peopled by one nation, speaking one language, professing one general system of religious and political principles, and accustomed to one general tenor of social usages and customs. For the common happiness of them all, for their peace and prosperity, I believe it is indispensable that they should be associated in one federal Union.” Source: John Quincy Adams, letter to his father, 1811 Source 2: “In assuming responsibilities so vast I fervently invoke the aid of that Almighty Ruler of the Universe in whose hands are the destinies of nations and of men to guard this Heaven-favored land against the mischiefs which without His guidance might arise from an unwise public policy. With a firm reliance upon the wisdom of Omnipotence to sustain and direct me in the path of duty which I am appointed to pursue, I stand in the presence of this assembled multitude of my countrymen to take upon myself the solemn obligation ‘to the best of my ability to preserve, protect, and defend the Constitution of the United States.” Source: James Polk, Inauguration Speech, 1845
options: (A) Whether or not newly admitted states ought to have the same amount of representation in Congress
(B) Whether or not Native Americans deserved equal rights in expanded American territory
(C) Whether or not slavery ought to be allowed in newly acquired territories
(D) Whether or not taxes should be raised to pay for new American territory
items.explanation: The only real controversy over taxes in the 1800s was over tariff policy, which had little to do with paying for new land (this never really came up as an issue), so eliminate (D). Supporters of Manifest Destiny saw no place for Native Americans in these lands, and there was little disagreement among policymakers here, eliminating (B). The question of representation in new states had been settled long ago with the Land Ordinances in the 1780s. Choice (C) is the best answer as the controversy over slavery was the biggest disagreement among American expansionists.

option_explanations.A: Representation for new states was settled by the Land Ordinances of the 1780s, which promised new states equality with the old — not a live controversy.
option_explanations.B: Expansionists broadly agreed Native Americans had no place in their vision of the continent; policymakers showed little disagreement on this.
option_explanations.C: Whether slavery could expand into newly acquired territory was the explosive question that split expansionists from the 1840s through the 1850s — Missouri, Texas, the Mexican Cession, Kansas.
option_explanations.D: Raising taxes to pay for new territory was never a real controversy; tariff policy was the era's tax fight, and it was unrelated to land purchases.

items.stem: Consistent with the image above, Irish immigrants to the United States during the 19th century largely sought out settlement within
items.stimulus: Density of Distribution of the Natives of Ireland: 1890, Government release of 11th Census Results, 1898. [Described: a pair of statistical maps (U.S. Census Office, 1898, public domain) showing where Irish-born residents lived in 1890. The darkest shading — the heaviest concentrations of Irish natives relative to population — falls over the industrial Northeast and the Great Lakes port cities, with far lighter shading across the rural South and the far West.]
options: (A) industrialized towns and cities
(B) plantations and mostly agrarian society
(C) the American West
(D) port cities
items.explanation: From the population density of Irish natives in the 1890 census, most immigrants settled in northern cities and towns where the economy was far more dependent upon industrialization. Plantations and agrarian society, (B), were far more common in the South, which saw comparatively little Irish immigration. The American West, (C), would see more immigration from Central and Eastern Europe during the mid- to late 19th century. While American port cities in New England saw massive populations of Irish immigrants, there was little immigration of Irish peoples into southern ports such as New Orleans and Charleston.

option_explanations.A: The 1890 census maps show the heaviest Irish concentrations in the industrial Northeast and Great Lakes cities — Irish immigrants settled overwhelmingly in industrialized towns and cities, where factory jobs were.
option_explanations.B: The rural South shows light Irish settlement on the maps; plantations and agrarian society were not where the Irish went.
option_explanations.C: The far West shows light Irish settlement; the maps' dark shading is in the East and Midwest, not the West.
option_explanations.D: Many Irish arrived through port cities, but the maps show them settling across the industrial belt — factories and cities generally, not port cities specifically. This understates the pattern shown.

items.stem: Which of the following would have the greatest impact on curbing immigration into the United States?
items.stimulus: Density of Distribution of the Natives of Ireland: 1890, Government release of 11th Census Results, 1898. [Described: a pair of statistical maps (U.S. Census Office, 1898, public domain) showing where Irish-born residents lived in 1890. The darkest shading — the heaviest concentrations of Irish natives relative to population — falls over the industrial Northeast and the Great Lakes port cities, with far lighter shading across the rural South and the far West.]
options: (A) Passage of the 13th and 14th Amendments
(B) The Chinese Exclusion Act of 1882
(C) The Immigration Act of 1924 (Johnson-Reed Act)
(D) The Naturalization Act of 1870
items.explanation: The Immigration Act of 1924 (Johnson-Reed Act) saw the United States set effective limits based on quotas for all immigration into the country. The passage of this act led to a significant reduction in immigration for all groups.

option_explanations.A: The 13th and 14th Amendments abolished slavery and defined citizenship — they did not restrict immigration.
option_explanations.B: The Chinese Exclusion Act (1882) barred one nationality only; it did not curb immigration generally.
option_explanations.C: The 1924 quota law set national-origins quotas that slashed immigration from all groups for decades — the single greatest curb on immigration into the United States.
option_explanations.D: The Naturalization Act of 1870 extended naturalization to people of African descent; it did not restrict immigration.

items.stem: How did European immigrants of the early and mid-19th century largely differ from those of the late 19th century?
items.stimulus: Density of Distribution of the Natives of Ireland: 1890, Government release of 11th Census Results, 1898. [Described: a pair of statistical maps (U.S. Census Office, 1898, public domain) showing where Irish-born residents lived in 1890. The darkest shading — the heaviest concentrations of Irish natives relative to population — falls over the industrial Northeast and the Great Lakes port cities, with far lighter shading across the rural South and the far West.]
options: (A) Earlier immigrants were generally fleeing religious and social persecution, whereas later immigrants were typically seeking out improved opportunities for work.
(B) Earlier immigrants were mostly from Western Europe, whereas later immigrants included more from Southern and Eastern Europe.
(C) Earlier immigrants were mostly Catholics, whereas later immigrants generally were more often Protestants.
(D) Earlier immigrants were highly educated, whereas later immigrants were poorly educated.
items.explanation: The majority of immigrants to the United States during the 1840s and 1850s were from Northern and Western Europe, whereas later immigrants during the 1890s–1920s were more frequently from Southern and Eastern Europe. The educational levels, (D), and religions of immigrants, (C), differed according to the specific regions that they came from. Their decision to immigrate to the United States in the 19th century was largely due to financial hardships and higher promise of jobs rather than religious persecution, (A).

option_explanations.A: Both waves were driven mainly by economic hardship and the promise of jobs, not primarily by fleeing religious persecution.
option_explanations.B: The early/mid-19th-century wave came largely from Northern and Western Europe (Irish, Germans); the late-19th-century wave (1890s-1920s) came increasingly from Southern and Eastern Europe (Italians, Poles, Russians, Jews).
option_explanations.C: This reverses the pattern. The early wave included many Irish Catholics; the later wave added more Catholics and Jews — not a shift toward Protestantism.
option_explanations.D: Education levels varied by specific group rather than by era; there was no clean early-educated/late-uneducated split.

items.stem: The policy referenced by the author above had which of the following impacts?
items.stimulus: “Some man who seemed to be a stranger (a United States officer, I presume) made a little speech and then read a rather long paper—the Emancipation Proclamation, I think. After the reading we were told that we were all free, and could go when and where we pleased. My mother, who was standing by my side, leaned over and kissed her children, while tears of joy ran down her cheeks. She explained to us what it all meant, that this was the day for which she had been so long praying, but fearing that she would never live to see.” Source: Booker T. Washington, Up From Slavery: An Autobiography , 1907
options: (A) It declared that all enslaved people in the United States were granted citizen rights.
(B) It declared that all enslaved people in states in open rebellion were free.
(C) It declared that slavery in Union-held territories was illegal.
(D) It declared that slavery throughout the United States was illegal.
items.explanation: The Emancipation Proclamation was meant to undermine the strength of the Confederate economies by encouraging enslaved people to flee and strengthen Union military support (many would go on to fight in the war). It did not grant citizen rights, (A), to freed enslaved people nor impact legality, (C) and (D), of slavery in free states (largely a measure not to push away border states, which remained in the Union, but were dependent upon slavery).

option_explanations.A: The Proclamation did not grant citizenship or citizen rights; that required the 14th Amendment (1868).
option_explanations.B: The Emancipation Proclamation (January 1, 1863) declared free all enslaved people in states 'in open rebellion' against the Union — a war measure aimed at the Confederacy's labor force.
option_explanations.C: Slavery in Union-held areas was explicitly exempted; Lincoln left the loyal border states' slavery untouched to keep them in the Union.
option_explanations.D: The Proclamation did not abolish slavery throughout the United States. Nationwide abolition required the 13th Amendment (1865).

items.stem: Northern opponents of Abraham Lincoln viewed the policy described above as
items.stimulus: “Some man who seemed to be a stranger (a United States officer, I presume) made a little speech and then read a rather long paper—the Emancipation Proclamation, I think. After the reading we were told that we were all free, and could go when and where we pleased. My mother, who was standing by my side, leaned over and kissed her children, while tears of joy ran down her cheeks. She explained to us what it all meant, that this was the day for which she had been so long praying, but fearing that she would never live to see.” Source: Booker T. Washington, Up From Slavery: An Autobiography , 1907
options: (A) a necessary step to end the Civil War
(B) an egregious attempt by the president to push unneeded social revolution
(C) a precursor to open rebellion by southern states over the nature of slavery
(D) an overly sympathetic gesture to the South
items.explanation: Copperheads were anti-war Democrats who opposed the ongoing war with the Confederacy and felt that President Lincoln was abusing his power of office, so eliminate (A). They viewed the Emancipation Proclamation as unnecessary and as an attempt by Lincoln to push his personal abolitionist views and social agenda to limit the power of the South, so eliminate (D). Copperheads emerged after the war had already begun, so eliminate (C).

option_explanations.A: Copperheads — anti-war Northern Democrats — opposed the war itself; they did not view the Proclamation as a necessary war measure.
option_explanations.B: Copperheads saw the Emancipation Proclamation as Lincoln abusing presidential power to force an unneeded social revolution and break Southern power — an egregious overreach, in their view.
option_explanations.C: The southern states had already rebelled in 1861, two years before the Proclamation; it cannot be a 'precursor' to a rebellion that already happened.
option_explanations.D: Copperheads were not sympathetic to the South; they opposed Lincoln's war policies, not out of Southern sympathy.

items.stem: Which of the following amendments to the U.S. Constitution provided the most federal legitimacy to the policy referenced above?
items.stimulus: “Some man who seemed to be a stranger (a United States officer, I presume) made a little speech and then read a rather long paper—the Emancipation Proclamation, I think. After the reading we were told that we were all free, and could go when and where we pleased. My mother, who was standing by my side, leaned over and kissed her children, while tears of joy ran down her cheeks. She explained to us what it all meant, that this was the day for which she had been so long praying, but fearing that she would never live to see.” Source: Booker T. Washington, Up From Slavery: An Autobiography , 1907
options: (A) The 13th Amendment
(B) The 14th Amendment
(C) The 15th Amendment
(D) The 16th Amendment
items.explanation: The 13th Amendment to the Constitution officially abolished slavery and involuntary servitude (except for punishment of a crime) in the United States. Passage of the 13th Amendment legitimized the decree of the Emancipation Proclamation and expanded its influence to the entirety of the country.

option_explanations.A: The 13th Amendment (1865) abolished slavery and involuntary servitude nationwide, giving permanent constitutional force to what the Proclamation — a wartime executive order — had decreed.
option_explanations.B: The 14th Amendment (1868) established citizenship and equal protection, but it was the 13th that abolished slavery itself.
option_explanations.C: The 15th Amendment (1870) protected voting rights; it did not abolish slavery.
option_explanations.D: The 16th Amendment (1913) authorized the income tax — unrelated to emancipation.

items.stem: Which of the following pieces of evidence from 1863 to 1900 could best be used to challenge the assertion made by the author in the passage?
items.stimulus: “Some man who seemed to be a stranger (a United States officer, I presume) made a little speech and then read a rather long paper—the Emancipation Proclamation, I think. After the reading we were told that we were all free, and could go when and where we pleased. My mother, who was standing by my side, leaned over and kissed her children, while tears of joy ran down her cheeks. She explained to us what it all meant, that this was the day for which she had been so long praying, but fearing that she would never live to see.” Source: Booker T. Washington, Up From Slavery: An Autobiography , 1907
options: (A) The passage of the Military Reconstruction Act
(B) The creation of the Freedmen’s Bureau
(C) The development of southern sharecropping
(D) Federal policies surrounding the Ku Klux Klan
items.explanation: To answer this question, you need to know what these answers are referencing. The Military Reconstruction Act saw the army enforcing the new Reconstruction amendments across the South, a boon for southern Black rights, so eliminate (A). The Freedman’s Bureau sought to provide work and education opportunities to newly freed slaves, eliminating (B). The federal government passed the Force Acts to target the Ku Klux Klan in the 1870s, removing (D). Southern sharecropping emerged as a continuation of the old system of cotton plantation labor, making (C) the best choice here.

option_explanations.A: The Military Reconstruction Act put the Army behind enforcing the new amendments across the South — a gain for Black rights that supports, not challenges, the freedom Washington describes.
option_explanations.B: The Freedmen's Bureau provided work, education, and aid to freed people — supporting, not challenging, the reality of emancipation.
option_explanations.C: Southern sharecropping trapped freed people in debt peonage and dependency — bondage by another name. It is the strongest evidence that emancipation did not deliver the genuine freedom Washington's mother celebrated.
option_explanations.D: The federal Force Acts of the 1870s targeted the Ku Klux Klan to protect Black rights — supporting, not challenging, emancipation's reality.

items.stem: Industrialists such as Andrew Carnegie’s opinion of the policy referenced above would most likely have been
items.stimulus: “Every contract, combination in the form of trust or otherwise, or conspiracy, in restraint of trade or commerce among the several States, or with foreign nations, is declared to be illegal…. Every person who shall monopolize, or attempt to monopolize, or combine or conspire with any other person or persons, to monopolize any part of the trade or commerce among the several States, or with foreign nations, shall be deemed guilty of a felony.” Source: Sherman Antitrust Act, 1890
options: (A) favorable, because it sought to prevent the formation of highly influential monopolies and trusts
(B) favorable, because it ensured that competition between companies would continue to regulate prices and political influence
(C) unfavorable, because it restricted capitalism
(D) unfavorable, because it concentrated the majority of wealth in the hands of a few
items.explanation: Andrew Carnegie was a business magnate who oversaw the steel industry and became one of the wealthiest industrialists in his time. He was a strong supporter of the principle of Social Darwinism and viewed the Sherman Antitrust Act negatively as it stifled capitalism.

option_explanations.A: Carnegie built his fortune through consolidation and monopoly; he would not favor a law aimed at breaking up combinations like his.
option_explanations.B: Carnegie did not want competition to regulate prices — he wanted to dominate markets through efficiency and scale.
option_explanations.C: Carnegie was a Social Darwinist who believed the efficient rightly triumphed. He viewed the Sherman Antitrust Act as an unnatural restriction on capitalism.
option_explanations.D: The Act did not concentrate wealth in a few hands — it aimed (however weakly) to break up concentration. Carnegie opposed it for restraining business, not for concentrating wealth.

items.stem: Which of the following is true of the policy referenced above?
items.stimulus: “Every contract, combination in the form of trust or otherwise, or conspiracy, in restraint of trade or commerce among the several States, or with foreign nations, is declared to be illegal…. Every person who shall monopolize, or attempt to monopolize, or combine or conspire with any other person or persons, to monopolize any part of the trade or commerce among the several States, or with foreign nations, shall be deemed guilty of a felony.” Source: Sherman Antitrust Act, 1890
options: (A) It represented a repudiation of midwestern state policies around trusts and monopolies.
(B) It had minimal effect on most industrial monopolies until the Progressive Era.
(C) It represented a significant victory for the organized labor movement.
(D) It dramatically reduced American economic growth at the turn of the century.
items.explanation: Midwestern states were already passing several laws targeting railroad rates and monopolies in the 1870s and 80s, so in many ways this is the federal government catching up to them; eliminate (A). This law was primarily used to attack labor unions rather than support them, so eliminate (C). Despite criticisms from industrialists (and a depression here and there), America’s economy still grew dramatically going into the Progressive Era, eliminating (D). Select (B) because this law was not really used to go after businesses until presidents like Teddy Roosevelt began invoking it to break up railroad trusts.

option_explanations.A: Midwestern states were already passing railroad and anti-monopoly laws in the 1870s and 80s. The federal act caught up to them; it did not repudiate them.
option_explanations.B: The Sherman Act was weakly and selectively enforced — famously turned against labor unions rather than trusts — and barely dented industrial monopolies until Theodore Roosevelt's Progressive-era prosecutions.
option_explanations.C: The Act was used against organized labor (e.g., the Danbury Hatters case), not a victory for it.
option_explanations.D: The American economy grew dramatically into the Progressive Era despite the Act; it did not reduce economic growth.

items.stem: Which of the following failed to strengthen the legality of the Sherman Antitrust Act?
items.stimulus: “Every contract, combination in the form of trust or otherwise, or conspiracy, in restraint of trade or commerce among the several States, or with foreign nations, is declared to be illegal…. Every person who shall monopolize, or attempt to monopolize, or combine or conspire with any other person or persons, to monopolize any part of the trade or commerce among the several States, or with foreign nations, shall be deemed guilty of a felony.” Source: Sherman Antitrust Act, 1890
options: (A) Passage of the Clayton Antitrust Act
(B) Passage of the Interstate Commerce Act
(C) Formation of the Federal Trade Commission
(D) Implementation of the McKinley Tariff
items.explanation: The McKinley Tariff (1890) imposed a high tariff on imports to protect domestic production and economic growth. However, this tariff had very little impact on the legality of the Sherman Antitrust Act and would have simply aided the existing big businesses in expanding their influence by reducing foreign competition. The Clayton Antitrust Act (1914), (A), Interstate Commerce Act (1887), (B), and formation of the FTC (1914), (C), all helped reign in abuses by big businesses and regulate domestic capitalism.

option_explanations.A: The Clayton Antitrust Act (1914) strengthened antitrust law and shielded unions — it supported, not failed, the Sherman Act's legality.
option_explanations.B: The Interstate Commerce Act (1887) began federal regulation of railroads — part of the same regulatory push, not a failure of it.
option_explanations.C: The Federal Trade Commission (1914) gave antitrust enforcement real teeth — it strengthened, not weakened, the regime.
option_explanations.D: The McKinley Tariff (1890) shielded domestic producers from foreign competition, helping big business grow. It did nothing to strengthen antitrust legality — this is the exception.

items.stem: The historical situation in relation to American antitrust policy in the period immediately before the passage of this act is most analogous to which of the following eras?
items.stimulus: “Every contract, combination in the form of trust or otherwise, or conspiracy, in restraint of trade or commerce among the several States, or with foreign nations, is declared to be illegal…. Every person who shall monopolize, or attempt to monopolize, or combine or conspire with any other person or persons, to monopolize any part of the trade or commerce among the several States, or with foreign nations, shall be deemed guilty of a felony.” Source: Sherman Antitrust Act, 1890
options: (A) The Progressive Era
(B) The New Deal Era
(C) The Great Society
(D) The Reagan Revolution
items.explanation: In the period leading up to the Sherman Antitrust Act, the government did little to counter trusts and mostly enforced a laissez-faire economic model. Look for a time period closest to that. Choice (A) can be eliminated because Progressives like Teddy Roosevelt strongly enforced antitrust law, as did Franklin Roosevelt during the New Deal Era, so eliminate (B). The Great Society in many ways continued the New Deal, removing (C). Ronald Reagan’s Supply Side Economics also saw the United States pull back dramatically on antitrust protections, so (D) is the correct answer.

option_explanations.A: The Progressive Era is the opposite parallel: Progressives like Theodore Roosevelt aggressively enforced antitrust law.
option_explanations.B: The New Deal Era is the opposite parallel: FDR vastly expanded federal economic intervention.
option_explanations.C: The Great Society continued New Deal-style federal intervention — the opposite of laissez-faire.
option_explanations.D: Before the Sherman Act, government did little about trusts under a laissez-faire model. That hands-off posture is most analogous to the Reagan Revolution's supply-side deregulation.

items.stem: Which of the following best characterizes the policies of Theodore Roosevelt as mentioned in the excerpt above?
items.stimulus: “It is not enough to be well-meaning and kindly, but weak; neither is it enough to be strong, unless morality and decency go hand in hand with strength. We must possess the qualities which make us do our duty in our homes and among our neighbors, and in addition we must possess the qualities which are indispensable to the make-up of every great and masterful nation—the qualities of courage and hardihood, of individual initiative and yet of power to combine for a common end, and above all, the resolute determination to permit no man and no set of men to sunder us one from the other by lines of caste or creed or section. We must act upon the motto of all for each and each for all. There must be ever present in our minds the fundamental truth that in a republic such as ours the only safety is to stand neither for nor against any man because he is rich or because he is poor, because he is engaged in one occupation or another, because he works with his brains or because he works with his hands. We must treat each man on his worth and merits as a man. We must see that each is given a square deal, because he is entitled to no more and should receive no less.” Source: Theodore Roosevelt, a speech to farmers in New York, 1903
options: (A) Reduced taxation on the lower class, enhanced protections for businesses, and isolationism on the global market
(B) Increased federal regulation of banking, tighter restrictions on trusts, and more support for domestic infrastructure
(C) Conservation of natural resources, control of corporations, and protection of consumers
(D) Radical social change, including enfranchisement of women and the prohibition of alcohol
items.explanation: Remember that the cornerstone to Roosevelt’s Square Deal was his three C’s: conservation of natural resources, control of corporations, and protection of consumers.

option_explanations.A: Reduced lower-class taxation, business protection, and isolationism do not describe Roosevelt's activist Square Deal.
option_explanations.B: Banking regulation and infrastructure support were not the Square Deal's defining formula.
option_explanations.C: The Square Deal's 'three C's' were conservation of natural resources, control of corporations, and protection of consumers.
option_explanations.D: Women's suffrage and prohibition were parallel reforms of the era, not the core of Roosevelt's Square Deal.

items.stem: The audience for Roosevelt’s speech likely would have been most supportive of which of the following policies of the Roosevelt administration?
items.stimulus: “It is not enough to be well-meaning and kindly, but weak; neither is it enough to be strong, unless morality and decency go hand in hand with strength. We must possess the qualities which make us do our duty in our homes and among our neighbors, and in addition we must possess the qualities which are indispensable to the make-up of every great and masterful nation—the qualities of courage and hardihood, of individual initiative and yet of power to combine for a common end, and above all, the resolute determination to permit no man and no set of men to sunder us one from the other by lines of caste or creed or section. We must act upon the motto of all for each and each for all. There must be ever present in our minds the fundamental truth that in a republic such as ours the only safety is to stand neither for nor against any man because he is rich or because he is poor, because he is engaged in one occupation or another, because he works with his brains or because he works with his hands. We must treat each man on his worth and merits as a man. We must see that each is given a square deal, because he is entitled to no more and should receive no less.” Source: Theodore Roosevelt, a speech to farmers in New York, 1903
options: (A) The creation of the National Parks system
(B) The break-up of the Northern Securities railroad trust
(C) The creation of the Food and Drug Administration
(D) The negotiation of settlements between organized labor and capital
items.explanation: All of these were part of Roosevelt’s Square Deal, so consider what a farmer would have been most supportive of. National Parks do go along with Roosevelt’s support of conserving the environment, but that would make little difference in the livelihood of farmers, so eliminate (A). The Pure Food and Drug Act was mostly a respond to muckrakers like Upton Sinclair’s The Jungle and the conditions in meatpacking factories, a more specifically urban problem, so eliminate (C). Ending strikes is again something that affects industrialists and union workers more, so eliminate (D). Choose (B) because farmers in the late 1800s organized most around regulating railroads and breaking up their monopolies, making this the correct choice.

option_explanations.A: National parks fit Roosevelt's conservationism but made little difference to farmers' livelihoods.
option_explanations.B: Farmers were squeezed by railroad monopolies' freight rates. Roosevelt's 1904 breakup of the Northern Securities railroad trust directly attacked the monopoly power farmers resented most.
option_explanations.C: The Pure Food and Drug Act answered urban muckraking about meatpacking (Sinclair's The Jungle) — a city problem, not a farmer's priority.
option_explanations.D: Settling strikes (as in the 1902 coal strike) mattered less to farmers than breaking the railroad trusts that controlled their shipping costs.

items.stem: In contrast to Roosevelt’s Square Deal, FDR’s First New Deal program aimed to
items.stimulus: “It is not enough to be well-meaning and kindly, but weak; neither is it enough to be strong, unless morality and decency go hand in hand with strength. We must possess the qualities which make us do our duty in our homes and among our neighbors, and in addition we must possess the qualities which are indispensable to the make-up of every great and masterful nation—the qualities of courage and hardihood, of individual initiative and yet of power to combine for a common end, and above all, the resolute determination to permit no man and no set of men to sunder us one from the other by lines of caste or creed or section. We must act upon the motto of all for each and each for all. There must be ever present in our minds the fundamental truth that in a republic such as ours the only safety is to stand neither for nor against any man because he is rich or because he is poor, because he is engaged in one occupation or another, because he works with his brains or because he works with his hands. We must treat each man on his worth and merits as a man. We must see that each is given a square deal, because he is entitled to no more and should receive no less.” Source: Theodore Roosevelt, a speech to farmers in New York, 1903
options: (A) improve crumbling domestic infrastructure
(B) provide work and stabilize the labor force
(C) restore confidence in the economy and banking system
(D) ensure financial support for retired and disabled workers
items.explanation: FDR’s First New Deal came at a time when the Great Depression crippled the United States and there remained fear of insecurity of banks and financial institutions. Much of his program aimed to restore confidence in banks and was successful in returning much needed money to banks to help stabilize the economy.

option_explanations.A: Infrastructure work was part of the New Deal, but the First New Deal's first aim was financial, not physical, reconstruction.
option_explanations.B: Providing work and stabilizing labor became central later; the First New Deal's opening priority was the banking system.
option_explanations.C: The First New Deal (1933) — the bank holiday, the FDIC, securities regulation — aimed first at restoring confidence in banks and the financial system so money would flow again.
option_explanations.D: Financial support for the retired and disabled came with Social Security in 1935, part of the Second New Deal, not the first.

items.stem: This excerpt from Article 231 of the Treaty of Versailles has been credited by some historians as contributing to the rise of Nazism and the later onset of World War II. All of the following have been provided as justifications of this view EXCEPT
items.stimulus: “The Allied and Associated Governments affirm and Germany accepts the responsibility of Germany and her allies for causing all the loss and damage to which the Allied and Associated Governments and their nationals have been subjected as a consequence of the war imposed upon them by the aggression of Germany and her allies.” Source: The Treaty of Versailles, Article 231, 1919
options: (A) the demand for war reparations led to rampant inflation in Germany
(B) establishing public indignation toward Allied governments for attributing full blame on Germany for World War I
(C) political instability with the abdication of the German monarchy
(D) formation of new formalized multinational alliances for protection and mutual interests
items.explanation: Following the First World War, there was fear that the standing alliances and formalized treaties that had led to the flair-up of the first war might ignite a second conflagration. Therefore, much more attention was applied toward diplomacy and negotiation through channels such as the League of Nations. Rampant inflation in Germany, (A), the fall of the monarchy, (C), and existing indignation toward the rest of Europe, (B), have all been credited with leading to the rise of Nazism in the 1920s and 1930s.

option_explanations.A: Reparations demands did help produce German hyperinflation in the early 1920s — a cited justification, not the exception.
option_explanations.B: The 'war guilt' clause did breed German indignation at the Allies — a cited justification, not the exception.
option_explanations.C: The Kaiser's abdication and the fragile Weimar Republic did create the instability extremists exploited — a cited justification, not the exception.
option_explanations.D: Postwar diplomacy moved away from entangling alliances toward the League of Nations. No new system of formalized multinational alliances was created as a result of Versailles — this is the exception.

items.stem: As a major part of the Treaty of Versailles, President Wilson sought to establish a League of Nations to
items.stimulus: “The Allied and Associated Governments affirm and Germany accepts the responsibility of Germany and her allies for causing all the loss and damage to which the Allied and Associated Governments and their nationals have been subjected as a consequence of the war imposed upon them by the aggression of Germany and her allies.” Source: The Treaty of Versailles, Article 231, 1919
options: (A) assemble an international forum for settling disputes through diplomacy and arbitration rather than war
(B) provide a stabilizing multinational security force to protect and defend international law
(C) counter future German aggression in Europe and Africa
(D) establish a common currency and international regulatory body for trade and economic growth
items.explanation: Wilson’s League of Nations proposal was meant to provide an international body to maintain peace and resolve conflicts through dialogue, diplomacy, and arbitration rather than armed conflict. The League of Nations would serve as a precursor to the United Nations that we have today.

option_explanations.A: Wilson envisioned the League of Nations as an international forum where disputes would be settled through diplomacy and arbitration rather than war — the forerunner of the United Nations.
option_explanations.B: The League had no real multinational security force to enforce international law; it depended on moral pressure and voluntary cooperation.
option_explanations.C: Countering future German aggression in Europe and Africa was not the League's stated purpose; it was a general peace-keeping body.
option_explanations.D: A common currency and international trade regulation were never the League's aims.

items.stem: In this excerpt, Truman advocates for an American doctrine of support in
items.stimulus: “The United States has received from the Greek Government an urgent appeal for financial and economic assistance…. The very existence of the Greek state is today threatened by the terrorist activities of several thousand armed men, led by Communists, who defy the government’s authority at a number of points, particularly along the northern boundaries…. Greece must have assistance if it is to become a self-supporting and self-respecting democracy…. One of the primary objectives of the foreign policy of the United States is the creation of conditions in which we and other nations will be able to work out a way of life free from coercion…. This is no more than a frank recognition that totalitarian regimes imposed on free peoples, by direct or indirect aggression, undermine the foundations of international peace and hence the security of the United States…. I believe that it must be the policy of the United States to support free peoples who are resisting attempted subjugation by armed minorities or by outside pressures.” Source: Harry Truman, speaking to a joint session of Congress, 1947
options: (A) international economic regulation and assistance for growing economies
(B) isolationism and neutrality to avoid future wars
(C) the recovery of nations destroyed in World War II
(D) opposing the growing geopolitical influence of communism
items.explanation: Truman’s request for support in Greece stemmed from his stance that the United States should oppose the growing geopolitical influence of communism sweeping through Europe and elsewhere in the world. While the United States did advocate for recovery of nations destroyed during World War II, (C), and improved economic regulation, (A), these concerns were minimal compared to the rising fears of communism.

option_explanations.A: International economic regulation was not Truman's subject. His appeal was about resisting communist coercion, not managing economies.
option_explanations.B: The doctrine was the opposite of isolationism: it committed the United States to active involvement abroad against communism.
option_explanations.C: Postwar recovery mattered (the Marshall Plan followed), but it was secondary to the doctrine's core purpose: stopping communist expansion.
option_explanations.D: The Truman Doctrine (1947) pledged American support to 'free peoples' resisting communist subjugation — first Greece and Turkey — making opposition to communism's geopolitical spread the doctrine's purpose.

items.stem: The argument made by Truman above was used to support U.S. intervention in all of the following from 1945 to 1980 EXCEPT
items.stimulus: “The United States has received from the Greek Government an urgent appeal for financial and economic assistance…. The very existence of the Greek state is today threatened by the terrorist activities of several thousand armed men, led by Communists, who defy the government’s authority at a number of points, particularly along the northern boundaries…. Greece must have assistance if it is to become a self-supporting and self-respecting democracy…. One of the primary objectives of the foreign policy of the United States is the creation of conditions in which we and other nations will be able to work out a way of life free from coercion…. This is no more than a frank recognition that totalitarian regimes imposed on free peoples, by direct or indirect aggression, undermine the foundations of international peace and hence the security of the United States…. I believe that it must be the policy of the United States to support free peoples who are resisting attempted subjugation by armed minorities or by outside pressures.” Source: Harry Truman, speaking to a joint session of Congress, 1947
options: (A) the Vietnam War in 1965
(B) the Hungarian Revolution in 1956
(C) the Cuban Bay of Pigs Invasion in 1961
(D) the Turkish Communist uprising of 1948
items.explanation: For this question, look for an example of the United States not using the Containment policy to intervene. The United States intervened in Vietnam, Cuba, and Turkey in these times under the theory that Truman puts forth above, but with the Hungarian uprising in 1956, the United States did not get involved for fear of further provoking the Soviets, making (B) the best answer.

option_explanations.A: The Vietnam escalation (1965) was justified under containment — Truman's logic applied, not the exception.
option_explanations.B: When Hungarians rose against Soviet domination in 1956, the United States stood aside for fear of provoking direct war with the USSR. Non-intervention here is the exception to the containment pattern.
option_explanations.C: The Bay of Pigs invasion (1961) was justified as stopping communism in Cuba — Truman's logic applied, not the exception.
option_explanations.D: Aid to Turkey against communist pressure (1948) was the Truman Doctrine's original application — not the exception.

items.stem: After 1980, the point of view expressed by Truman is most apparent in
items.stimulus: “The United States has received from the Greek Government an urgent appeal for financial and economic assistance…. The very existence of the Greek state is today threatened by the terrorist activities of several thousand armed men, led by Communists, who defy the government’s authority at a number of points, particularly along the northern boundaries…. Greece must have assistance if it is to become a self-supporting and self-respecting democracy…. One of the primary objectives of the foreign policy of the United States is the creation of conditions in which we and other nations will be able to work out a way of life free from coercion…. This is no more than a frank recognition that totalitarian regimes imposed on free peoples, by direct or indirect aggression, undermine the foundations of international peace and hence the security of the United States…. I believe that it must be the policy of the United States to support free peoples who are resisting attempted subjugation by armed minorities or by outside pressures.” Source: Harry Truman, speaking to a joint session of Congress, 1947
options: (A) the Western-backed invasion of Iraq in 2003
(B) the signing of the INF treaty with the Soviets in 1987
(C) the United Nations intervention against Saddam Hussein in 1991
(D) the signing of the North American Free Trade Agreement in 1994
items.explanation: Here, Truman is saying that the United States has a duty to “support free peoples” abroad. The signing of the INF treaty represents a collaboration with the Soviet Union, something that doesn’t really go with Truman’s combative posture against the Soviets, removing (B). NAFTA is a trade policy and not so much a military one, so eliminate (D). While (C) might be tempting, the United States had brought international support against Saddam Hussein (including Russia) in 1991, so (A) is the best choice: it represents America going alone with its Western allies and intervening similarly to how Truman suggests in the passage.

option_explanations.A: The 2003 Western invasion of Iraq was justified in part as liberating Iraqis from tyranny — Truman's 'support free peoples' rationale applied unilaterally, the clearest post-1980 echo of the doctrine's combative posture.
option_explanations.B: The INF Treaty (1987) was collaboration with the Soviet Union, not Truman-style confrontation of it.
option_explanations.C: The 1991 Gulf War coalition was broad and international (even Russia cooperated) and aimed at expelling Iraq from Kuwait — less the unilateral moral crusade of Truman's doctrine.
option_explanations.D: NAFTA (1994) is a trade agreement, not a military commitment to free peoples.

items.stem: All of the following were new programs and initiatives instituted as a part of Johnson’s Great Society EXCEPT
items.stimulus: “Your imagination, your initiative, and your indignation will determine whether we build a society where progress is the servant of our needs, or a society where old values and new visions are buried under unbridled growth. For in your time we have the opportunity to move not only toward the rich society and the powerful society, but upward to the Great Society. “The Great Society rests on abundance and liberty for all. It demands an end to poverty and racial injustice, to which we are totally committed in our time. But that is just the beginning. “The Great Society is a place where every child can find knowledge to enrich his mind and to enlarge his talents. It is a place where leisure is a welcome chance to build and reflect, not a feared cause of boredom and restlessness. It is a place where the city of man serves not only the needs of the body and the demands of commerce but the desire for beauty and the hunger for community.” Source: Lyndon B. Johnson, commencement speech, 1964
options: (A) the Civil Rights Act
(B) the Economic Opportunity Act
(C) the Voting Rights Act
(D) the Social Security Act
items.explanation: While much of his attention was aimed at several of the same goals as the Social Security Act, this legislation was actually passed during the presidency of FDR. The Civil Rights Act, (A), Economic Opportunity Act, (B), and Voting Rights Act, (C), were all major acts passed during the Johnson presidency that had considerable impacts on American society.

option_explanations.A: The Civil Rights Act (1964) was a Great Society landmark — not the exception.
option_explanations.B: The Economic Opportunity Act (1964), launching the War on Poverty, was a Great Society landmark — not the exception.
option_explanations.C: The Voting Rights Act (1965) was a Great Society landmark — not the exception.
option_explanations.D: The Social Security Act (1935) was Franklin Roosevelt's New Deal, three decades earlier — not part of Johnson's Great Society. This is the exception.

items.stem: The domestic policy and vision of the Great Society aligns most closely with which of the following political stances today?
items.stimulus: “Your imagination, your initiative, and your indignation will determine whether we build a society where progress is the servant of our needs, or a society where old values and new visions are buried under unbridled growth. For in your time we have the opportunity to move not only toward the rich society and the powerful society, but upward to the Great Society. “The Great Society rests on abundance and liberty for all. It demands an end to poverty and racial injustice, to which we are totally committed in our time. But that is just the beginning. “The Great Society is a place where every child can find knowledge to enrich his mind and to enlarge his talents. It is a place where leisure is a welcome chance to build and reflect, not a feared cause of boredom and restlessness. It is a place where the city of man serves not only the needs of the body and the demands of commerce but the desire for beauty and the hunger for community.” Source: Lyndon B. Johnson, commencement speech, 1964
options: (A) Liberals
(B) Evangelicals
(C) Moderates
(D) Conservatives
items.explanation: President Johnson was a Democrat and a liberal. His policies of greater government involvement in socioeconomic reforms and social change align closely to the stance of modern liberals.

option_explanations.A: Johnson was a liberal Democrat whose Great Society vastly expanded federal involvement in social welfare — the stance that aligns most closely with modern liberals.
option_explanations.B: Evangelicals tend toward social conservatism, which opposes the Great Society's liberal expansion of federal power.
option_explanations.C: Moderates sit between the poles; the closest alignment for the Great Society vision is with liberals, not the middle.
option_explanations.D: Conservatives oppose the Great Society's expanded federal role in socioeconomic life — the opposite alignment.
